title: One great body
hook: we are members of one great body; nature made us kin (Letters 95)

segments.voice: Yesterday: what learning is for. Your line was what is it for. Which lesson did you ask, and what did it turn out to be for? Day four hundred seventy-eight.
screen: `WHAT LEARNING IS FOR — WHAT IS IT FOR.`

segments.voice: Stub your toe and your whole body reacts. Your hand reaches down, your face winces, your other foot takes the weight. Nobody holds a meeting. Nobody says: not my department, I'm a hand. The parts just know they belong to each other. The ninety-fifth letter is a long, dense argument about rules and principles in ethics. But near the end, he stops arguing and offers Lucilius a single formula for how we should treat every other human being. It begins with the body. Today: one great body.
screen: `STUB YOUR TOE.` → `NOBODY SAYS: NOT MY DEPARTMENT.` → `ONE FORMULA FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In Latin: membra sumus corporis magni. We are the limbs of one great body. Everything you see, divine and human, Seneca says, is one, and we are members of it. Second, kinship. Nature made us relatives, he says, since she made us from the same materials and for the same ends. She gave us a love for one another and made us fit for living together. She set up fairness and justice. By her law, it's worse to harm than to be harmed. Third, a line from the stage. Seneca quotes a verse from the Roman playwright Terence, and tells Lucilius to keep it on his lips and in his heart: I am human; I count nothing human foreign to me. Whatever happens to any person is my concern. Fourth, the arch. Our life together, he says, is like an arch of stones, which would fall if the stones didn't hold each other up. That's how it stands at all. Stoic teachers had a word for this widening belonging, oikeiosis: care that starts with your own body can grow, they taught, to take in the whole human race. A stranger at a bus stop is a stone in your arch.
screen: `MEMBRA SUMUS CORPORIS MAGNI.` · `NATURE MADE US KIN.` · `NOTHING HUMAN IS FOREIGN TO ME.` · `AN ARCH OF STONES.` · then, large: `ONE BODY.`

segments.voice: Feel your own body for a moment: hands, feet, the breath moving through the middle. All of it working together without being asked. Now widen the circle. Picture someone you love. Then someone you see often but barely know. Then a stranger somewhere far away, waking up or going to sleep right now. Same materials, same breath, same short life. Hold the whole widening circle as one body. The bell holds the time.
One great body. Seneca's membra sumus corporis magni: we are limbs of one great body, made kin by nature, holding each other up like stones in an arch. Today's word.
Your line: one body. Help one stranger today: hold a door, give directions, pick up what they dropped. The hand doesn't ask whose foot it is. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Stoic practitioners sometimes picture widening circles of concern, from self to family to strangers to all people, and act on that by helping someone they don't know.

fork.reveal: Seneca says we're members of one great body; like stones in an arch, we stand only by holding each other up.

original.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 95.52: we are the limbs of a great body.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice image of togetherness.
what it means: all people are kin by nature, parts of one body, and harming another is worse than being harmed.
what a scholar hears: Letters 95.51–53; Terence, Heauton Timorumenos 77 ('homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto'); the Stoic idea of oikeiosis, later pictured by Hierocles as concentric circles.

notes: Letters 95.52: 'omne hoc quod vides... unum est; membra sumus corporis magni. Natura nos cognatos edidit...'; 'miserius est nocere quam laedi'. 95.53: Terence's verse and the arch ('societas nostra lapidum fornicationi simillima est'). Confirm.
Terence's line paraphrased in English (no PD translation cited); Latin given only in the trapdoor.
Oikeiosis and Hierocles' circles (in Stobaeus): confirm the trapdoor wording. Seneca does not use the Greek term in this letter; the script attributes it to 'Stoics'.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced superlative 'one of the longest Seneca wrote'; reworded the oikeiosis gloss as a Stoic teaching rather than a hope stated as fact.
